slides.q: Why do I sometimes wake up and can't move?
slides.a: That's sleep paralysis. Your mind wakes up while your body is still in the dream-stage 'off switch' that stops you acting out dreams. It's terrifying but harmless, and usually passes within a minute or two. It's more likely when you're short on sleep or stressed. Worth seeing a doctor if it happens a lot.

slides.q: Why have my dreams been so vivid lately?
slides.a: Stress is a big one, and so is broken sleep. When you wake up more often, you're more likely to remember dreams. After a stretch of poor sleep or drinking, your brain can also catch up on dream sleep, making dreams more intense. Some medications do it too. Worth mentioning to a doctor if nightmares wreck your sleep.

slides.q: Why do I grind my teeth at night?
slides.a: It's called bruxism, and stress is one of the most common triggers. Caffeine, alcohol, and some sleep problems can make it worse. Signs include a sore jaw, morning headaches, or worn teeth. A dentist can fit you with a night guard to protect them. Worth asking a doctor too if you also snore loudly or wake up exhausted.

slides.q: Why do I wake up right before my alarm?
slides.a: Your body clock is better than you think. If you wake at roughly the same time each day, your body learns the pattern and starts ramping up wake-up hormones like cortisol before the alarm goes off. Even expecting an early start can nudge you awake. It's a sign your schedule is fairly consistent, which is good.

slides.q: Why do I sleep so much better when it's raining?
slides.a: Rain is a steady, gentle sound that works like natural white noise. It masks sudden noises, like cars or doors, that would otherwise jolt you awake. Plus, a cozy room and a grey sky make winding down feel easier. If it works for you, a rain sounds track at night is a totally valid sleep hack.
